title: CROSS: Compiler-Driven Optimization of Sparse DNNs Using Sparse/Dense Computation Kernels
problem: Exploiting DNN weight sparsity on GPUs is hindered by the overhead of index-based encoding/decoding required by sparse formats, making sparse computation kernels slower than dense kernels even at high sparsity ratios.
motivation: As DNN models grow larger, sparsity is critical for reducing inference cost, but the gap between theoretical sparsity speedup and actual GPU performance prevents practical adoption of diverse sparsity patterns.
method: CROSS is a compiler that analyzes where nonzero weights cluster together in a neural network (parameter distribution locality) to identify sections where dense computation remains fast. It splits sparse neural network computation into pieces at different sparsity levels and routes each piece to either a specialized sparse kernel or an optimized dense kernel. The framework translates the sparse computation graph into a form that works with high-performance dense GPU routines (BLAS-level operations), avoiding the expensive overhead of sparse index encoding while still skipping zero values. It handles various sparsity patterns: unstructured (random zero distribution), structured (entire rows or columns of zeros), and N:M (exactly M nonzeros per N values).
key_novelty: CROSS exploits weight clustering (parameter distribution locality) and sparse graph translation to run sparse neural networks efficiently on dense GPU kernels, avoiding sparse format overhead while still skipping zero computations.
contributions: In-depth analysis of sparse operation patterns in mainstream DNN computing frameworks identifying locality-exploitable regions
CROSS framework decomposing sparse workloads into multi-sparsity components mapped to sparse or dense kernels
Sparse graph translation technique enabling dense computation kernels to process sparse workloads
Average 2.03x speedup on inference latency compared to seven state-of-the-art solutions with smaller memory footprints
limitations: The approach relies on parameter distribution locality being present; highly irregular or truly random sparsity patterns may limit applicability of the dense kernel reconciliation.
primary_theme: compiler-driven sparse-dense kernel co-optimization for sparse DNN GPU inference
